significance.justification: A verified-true result would establish the form-(iii) law that repetition count "monotonically inflates" internally decoded belief even for false claims, together with a form-(ii) mechanism in which a causally separable "familiarity/fluency" component can be ablated without removing truth representation. This establishes both a phenomenon and a mechanism: it predicts belief shifts across repetition doses and truth values, while the dissociation would change whether redundant contextual evidence can be interpreted as independent support; this matters against the established human effect in Fazio et al. (2015) and the truth-representation substrate studied by Marks and Tegmark's Geometry of Truth. True and false are determinate, and a clean negative dose-response would informatively rule out repetition as a general source of internal belief inflation, although failure of only the localization branch would merely favor a distributed or entangled mechanism. Topic-substitution check: replacing these specific dose-response and causal-dissociation claims with generic research on LLM beliefs would not justify this score, so the rating comes from the constraining law and decomposition rather than the topic.

reach.justification: The transferable handles named by the claim are "per-count belief/confidence dose-response slopes," the "familiarity/fluency" component, and an intervention where "ablating it restores truth-tracking." The internal slope can operate ex ante—after reading a repetitive context but before issuing the behavioral truth judgment—while ablation supplies a deployment-time control rather than only a post-hoc explanation. After per-model re-extraction, the monotonic, truth-independent dose-response predicts a relation that should recur, although the exact direction or heads must be rediscovered; the asserted scope covers multiple domains, real and synthetic claims, and open-weight transformer families, but explicitly does not ensure transfer to very large closed models. Auditors of retrieval or repeated-user contexts could use the signal to flag or suppress repetition-induced belief shifts, and the topic-substitution check shows that generic belief research alone would not provide this predictor or intervention.
